# ADR-0012 — Seats are generated by their parent, not stored individually

**Status:** Accepted · 2026-08-08

## Context

[ADR-0001](ADR-0001-rendering.md) chose a hand-rolled Canvas2D renderer, with a
stated reversal condition: **"realistic scenes exceed ~5,000 objects"**. Open
Question 1 in [RESEARCH.md](../RESEARCH.md) existed to find that number before
Phase 3 committed to the renderer.

Answering it exposed that "objects" was hiding two different quantities:

- **Elements** — what the document holds, what the spatial index stores, what
  hit-testing narrows against, what undo operates on.
- **Drawn primitives** — what the renderer actually paints each frame.

A ten-seat round table is **one element** and **eleven shapes**. Which number
matters depends entirely on how seats are represented, and that had never been
decided.

### Evidence

| Source                         | Figure                                                             |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Industry planning guidance     | 1,000 guests ≈ 125 round tables                                    |
| Grand Hyatt Hong Kong ballroom | 1,248 banquet / 2,016 theatre                                      |
| Hyatt Regency Denver           | 3,000 seated                                                       |
| Marriott Marquis DC            | 3,500 theatre-style — among the largest anywhere                   |
| Cvent, SeatPlan, Prismm        | No published object limit; one review notes "large models can lag" |

CAD practice splits the same way the data does: individual chair blocks for
flexible seating, table-and-chair groupings for structured banquets.

## Decision

**Seats are generated by the element that owns them. They are never stored as
independent elements.**

- A table carries a `seats` count. Its chairs are laid out procedurally around
  it at render time.
- Theatre, classroom, and ceremony rows become a **seating block** element
  (rows × columns, with aisle spacing) that generates its chairs the same way.
  Phase 5 builds it; recorded here so it is designed rather than discovered.
- A seat is addressed as `(elementId, seatIndex)` — it has identity without
  having an element. Guest assignment in Phase 7 references that pair.

### Resulting scale

| Scenario                 | Elements | Drawn primitives |
| ------------------------ | -------- | ---------------- |
| Wedding, 150 guests      | ~30      | ~200             |
| Large gala, 1,250 guests | ~190     | ~1,450           |
| Theatre, 3,500 seats     | ~50      | ~3,600           |
| Expo hall, 500 booths    | ~520     | ~1,100           |

**Elements stay under ~1,000 in every realistic plan.** Drawn primitives reach
about 4,000 at the top end; 6,000 allowing for decoration and annotation.

## Consequences

**[ADR-0001](ADR-0001-rendering.md) holds. Its reversal condition is not met**,
and by a wide margin — realistic element counts are roughly a fifth of the
threshold that would have forced WebGL.

The benchmark comparison that drove ADR-0001 (Konva 23 fps, Fabric 9 fps at
8,000 objects) measured _interactive scene-graph nodes_, each carrying event
handling and transform state. Our 4,000 primitives are immediate-mode fills with
no per-shape overhead, because chairs are not individually interactive — clicking
a chair selects its table. These are different regimes, and the comparison
flatters our case rather than threatening it.

**Phase 3 benchmark targets**, set by this ADR:

| Measure                       | Target |
| ----------------------------- | ------ |
| Elements in the spatial index | 1,000  |
| Drawn primitives per frame    | 5,000  |
| Sustained pan/zoom            | 60 fps |
| Hit-test                      | < 1 ms |

**A seat count is not a chair count.** Changing a table from 8 seats to 10 must
not orphan guest assignments. Phase 7 defines what happens to a guest in seat 9
when the table shrinks; the seat index makes that a defined case rather than a
dangling reference.

**Individually placed chairs remain possible** — a loose chair by a doorway is
just a fixture. What is ruled out is _modelling a 300-seat ceremony as 300
elements_, which would inflate the index, the file, and the undo stack for no
benefit a seating block does not already provide.

## Rejected alternatives

| Option                                               | Why not                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Chairs as independent elements**                   | 3,500-element documents for a theatre layout, an index and undo stack to match, and a file that is mostly repeated chair records. Buys per-chair positioning that no planner asked for. |
| **Chairs as child elements with a parent reference** | A hierarchy in the document model, and every operation — move, delete, undo, serialize — has to reason about it. Procedural generation gets the same result with no tree.               |
| **Deciding later**                                   | The choice determines the Phase 3 benchmark target, and therefore whether ADR-0001 survives. Deferring it means benchmarking against a guess.                                           |

## Reverse if

A real workflow needs per-chair positioning inside a seated group — moving one
chair at a table for a wheelchair space is the plausible case. That is better
solved by per-seat overrides on the parent element than by promoting every chair
to an element, so even then this decision likely stands.
